title: Brazil's Federal Police Froze Up to R$54 Billion in the Second Phase of Operation Disclosure. The Targets Include the Sons of Jorge Paulo Lemann and Three Named Banks. Itaú Says It Refused the Balance-Confirmation Letter Alteration the Police Allege Occurred. The Other Two Banks Have Not Said the Same.
narrative:
On Thursday June 25 2026, Brazil's Federal Police launched the second phase of Operation Disclosure, an investigation into alleged accounting fraud and market manipulation at retailer Americanas S.A. Authorities executed nine search-and-seizure warrants in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo; the court ordered the freezing of up to R$54 billion in assets. The named targets span three layers of the alleged fraud: controlling shareholders (Carlos Alberto Sicupira), former board members (Eduardo Saggioro; Paulo Alberto Lemann, son of Jorge Paulo Lemann), and — for the first time at this scope — three named banks whose officers allegedly cooperated in the concealment (Itaú Unibanco: José Rudge and Gustavo Balassiano; Bradesco: Carlos Henrique Villela Pedras; Santander: Sérgio Rial — the former Santander chairman who briefly served as Americanas CEO in January 2023 — and André Almeida and Alexandre Abdo).

The underlying fraud scheme: Americanas allegedly concealed R$20+ billion in supplier-financing obligations — the so-called 'risco sacado' vehicle — from its financial statements, and falsified cooperative advertising allowance agreements recorded 'without underlying economic substance,' producing financial results and leverage indicators that appeared significantly stronger than reality. On January 11 2023, the newly appointed CEO Rial disclosed R$20 billion in accounting inconsistencies and resigned immediately with CFO André Covre. The Federal Police now suspect a criminal organization led by former CEO Miguel Gutierrez, involving approximately 60 individuals, that manipulated financial results by roughly R$25 billion. Federal prosecutors in late March 2025 had already charged 13 executives including Gutierrez, Anna Saicali, José Timotheo de Barros, and Márcio Cruz.

The new phase extends the scrutiny to the bank layer. The Federal Police evidence, per Valor International, includes emails and messages between Americanas executives and bank officials alleging that Americanas management 'sought to persuade lenders not to classify supplier-financing transactions as debt in balance-confirmation letters sent to auditing firms.' The investigation also targets Sicupira and the board members who served during the period — an allegation they have consistently denied.

Itaú Unibanco, 'not under investigation,' issued a categorical denial on June 25: it 'has actively cooperated with authorities since 2023' and 'the records clearly show that Itaú refused requests from Americanas's former management to alter balance-confirmation letters.' Bradesco said it is 'monitoring the case.' Americanas said it 'will continue to cooperate with the investigations.'

analysis:
The R$54 billion asset freeze in Operação Disclosure Phase 2 is the first time the Americanas fraud investigation has reached the bank layer at this scope — three named banks, five named bank officers, and the controlling shareholder / former board-member layer of Americanas itself. The load-bearing structural finding sits on the balance-confirmation letter, the document Americanas allegedly asked lenders not to alter in correspondence with its auditing firm.

The Federal Police allegation, as Valor International reported, is that Americanas management 'sought to persuade lenders not to classify supplier-financing transactions as debt in balance-confirmation letters sent to auditing firms.' This is a specific factual claim about the mechanism of the fraud: the R$20+ billion in 'risco sacado' supplier-financing obligations was concealed in part by securing lender cooperation in misclassifying them on the documents the auditor relied on. If the police theory is correct, at least one of the three named banks — Itaú, Bradesco, or Santander — was persuaded to alter its letter. If no bank was persuaded, the police theory about the fraud mechanism has a gap.

Itaú's June 25 categorical denial addresses this point directly: 'the records clearly show that Itaú refused requests from Americanas's former management to alter balance-confirmation letters.' This is a strong denial, and it makes Itaú's absence from the formal investigation list ('although not under investigation') internally consistent. But it does not address the question of whether Bradesco or Santander refused in the same way Itaú claims to have refused.

Bradesco has said only that it is 'monitoring the case.' Santander has not, in the June 25 reporting, issued a categorical statement of any kind. The Federal Police have named three Santander individuals (Rial, Almeida, Abdo) and one Bradesco individual (Villela Pedras) as targets. Under the police theory, these named bank officers were targets because they cooperated in the balance-confirmation letter alteration; under Itaú's denial framing, they were targets because Americanas management made requests to them that may have been refused (in which case they would be witnesses, not co-conspirators, and the warrant targeting would be overreach).

The structural finding is the asymmetry between the police allegation and the bank response. Either (a) at least one of the three named banks was persuaded to alter its balance-confirmation letter — which makes the fraud mechanism cross-bank, not Itaú-only, and which means the 'concealment' layer was effective at the bank level for at least one of the three — or (b) no bank was persuaded, in which case the police theory about the concealment mechanism is incomplete, and the Santander and Bradesco individuals were targeted for refusing rather than cooperating (in which case the warrants are investigating refused requests, not successful ones, and the 'criminal organization' framing is harder to sustain against the bank layer).

The Brazilian corporate-disclosure beat is fresh ground for the siphoned-truth archive. The closest prior articles on the markets-finance / corporate-disclosure umbrella are the OpenAI audited-statement leak (US-Domiciled, audited-statement non-disclosure) and the Gildan channel-stuffing story (US-Domiciled, inventory overhang). The Americanas case is Brazilian-Domiciled, the mechanism is the 'risco sacado' supplier-financing vehicle — a Brazilian-market-specific instrument that lets retailers finance working capital through reverse factoring of supplier receivables — and the law-enforcement posture is Operação Disclosure of the Brazilian Federal Police, not BFA Law's US private investigation. The Digimais Operation Mirage article from June 23 covers a different Brazilian banking fraud (a religious-media R$670 million freeze tied to a BTG Pactual acquisition jeopardy) and is structurally distinct from Americanas. Americanas is a new beat within the Brazilian corporate-disclosure sub-cluster.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: On Thursday June 25 2026, Brazil's Federal Police launched the second phase of Operation Disclosure with nine search-and-seizure warrants in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo and a court-ordered freeze of up to R$54 billion in assets. The targets span three layers of the alleged fraud: the controlling shareholder (Carlos Alberto Sicupira), the former board (Saggioro, Paulo Alberto Lemann), and — for the first time at this scope — three named banks (Itaú: Rudge + Balassiano; Bradesco: Villela Pedras; Santander: Rial + Almeida + Abdo). The load-bearing structural finding is the balance-confirmation letter dispute: the Federal Police allege Americanas management 'sought to persuade lenders not to classify supplier-financing transactions as debt in balance-confirmation letters sent to auditing firms'; Itaú's categorical denial states 'the records clearly show that Itaú refused requests from Americanas's former management to alter balance-confirmation letters.' Both cannot be true at the level of fact — yet three named Santander individuals and one Bradesco individual are also in the target list. Either at least one of those three banks was persuaded (which makes the fraud mechanism cross-bank, not Itaú-only), or the police allegation is about pressure without effect (which would not justify including the Santander and Bradesco individuals in the second phase). Beat-distinct from the OpenAI audited-statement leak (US-Domiciled audited-statement non-disclosure; Americanas is Brazilian-Domiciled concealment of supplier-financing debt) and the Gildan channel-stuffing inventory overhang (US-Domiciled channel-stuffing; Americanas is Brazilian-Domiciled cross-bank balance-confirmation letter dispute). The risco sacado supplier-financing mechanism is a Brazilian-market-specific fraud vehicle the siphoned-truth archive has not yet covered.
